title: Crowd-Sourced Reviews of Aid Delivery: A Distant Dream or a Soon-to-Be Reality?
html:
The challenges around collecting feedback from those affected by a crisis have been a common topic of discussion for many years. BBC’s 2012 Still Left in the Dark? noted that research findings from 2006 in Aceh and Sri Lanka (2004 tsunami) remained valid nearly a decade later. Most agencies were paralyzed with fear: fear of not being able to answer all the questions, fear of lacking the skill and capacity to handle the volume of feedback, fear of angry or critical feedback. The Red Cross’ 2013 World Disaster Reports: Focus on Technology and the Future of Humanitarian Action raised the need for feedback channels, but cautioned that beneficiaries are often disgruntled and upset when they do not receive immediate results or feedback after offering opinions or concerns.

In 2014, Mark Turner reached out to the CrisisMappers email group suggesting the idea of AidAdvisor - an online review aggregator similar to TripAdvisor, aimed to collect feedback from aid recipients. The benefits are easy to imagine and range from adjusting an organization’s response to transparency, to donor allotment adjustments. But, there would also be many challenges from possible bias to verification requirements, to internet access to quality control, to abuse of the system.

Over the years, different groups have suggested or set up different evaluation systems - AidEvaluator, Disaster Accountability, multiple call centers by different UN agencies, social media response through American Red Cross digital volunteer network, and so on.  Yet, nothing has managed to grow into the sector-wide, transparent solution that Mark proposed.

In this regard, I posed a question to Jeremy Andrews this past summer: Could modern technology - especially artificial intelligence - provide a solution to the many problems outlined? Or, could we identify another simple solution as a first step in building a sector-wide, transparent one? We have outlined our findings in Crowd-Sourced Reviews of the Aid Delivery: A Distant Dream or a Soon-to-Be Reality.

[PDF]

Although artificial intelligence does provide exciting possibilities, its ability is expected to take a major step forward in the next 12-18 months so the community would likely be better placed spending donors’ money elsewhere at the moment.

Perhaps that better place is paying for and implementing a simple solution like HappyOrNot. Focus on specific interactions, gain very rapid feedback through a cloud-based data analytics service, and begin sharing that information and stories with the public.

Andrej

A special thanks to Alona Volinsky for her editorial work and Ignacio G. Rebollo for his design work.
teaser: Why crowd-sourced reviews of aid delivery are hard, from bias to verification, and a possible approach using quick feedback on specific interactions.
seo_description: Challenges and benefits of collecting feedback from aid recipients, existing evaluation systems and a proposed rapid-feedback approach.
